tldr: LiteReality-Agent is an AI agent system that reconstructs entire interactive, simulation-ready 3D indoor scenes from RGB-D scans captured with a smartphone or tablet. By formulating the entire room as a single executable Python script (Room.py), a coding agent iteratively executes an observe-edit-verify loop to automatically build high-quality digital twins free of penetrations and floating objects.
hero_caption: The overall pipeline of LiteReality-Agent. From scan data, initial layout defects are repaired to produce an initial Room.py. A coding agent then iteratively refines the Python script through visual observation, measurement, rendering comparison, and verification gates.
overview:
Bringing real-world rooms directly into simulators is in high demand for robot learning and digital twins, but existing 3D reconstruction techniques face serious hurdles. Methods like NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting look visually stunning, yet they lack meshes and physical properties. Meanwhile, conventional mesh reconstruction often produces interpenetrating or floating furniture, making direct physical simulation impractical.

To overcome this, the authors formulated 3D room reconstruction as a coding problem. The entire room is represented as a single executable Blender/Python script, Room.py, which an LLM-based coding agent iteratively edits. Grounded in real-world RGB-D scan imagery, the agent writes furniture placements, wall textures, and lighting into code. It then inspects and corrects its code by comparing rendered views against real photos (rendering inspection). Furthermore, quality gates strictly verify furniture collisions and surface grounding, automatically preventing physical defects.

Experiments across 10 real-world scenes, including offices and kitchens, evaluated the approach against frontier LLM baselines (such as GPT-6 and Claude Fable 5.1) running out-of-the-box, as well as the prior method LiteReality. LiteReality-Agent significantly outperformed baselines not only in visual fidelity (PSNR and LPIPS) but also in physical validity metrics like geometric depth error, ground contact rate, and mesh intersection count. The resulting environments can be exported directly into the MuJoCo simulator, ready for immediate robotic arm manipulation experiments.
contributions: Formulated whole-room 3D reconstruction as continuous refactoring of an executable Python script (Room.py), offering an intuitive, editable workspace for both humans and AI.
Developed a suite of observe-edit-verify tools and workflows that combine real-world RGB-D evidence gathering, local and global rendering inspection, and metric wall-grid measurements.

Introduced geometric and physical consistency quality gates (collision and support checks) to eliminate interpenetrations and floating furniture, enabling instant export to simulators like MuJoCo without manual cleanup.

sections.heading: Why is interactive 3D indoor reconstruction so hard for robotics?
sections.summary: Automatically building physics-ready digital twins from real spaces has long been a dream in robotics. However, simultaneously handling object articulation, physical property estimation, and layout consistency end-to-end has proved exceptionally difficult. This paper tackles the challenge by treating the entire room as executable Python code.
sections.details:
Point clouds, NeRF, and 3D Gaussians yield visually appealing results, but they do not provide the structured environments needed for robots to interact with objects and compute physics. On the other hand, CAD retrieval methods and single-pass generative pipelines struggle to generalize to diverse furniture types and complex, non-standard room configurations.

Recently, research using LLMs to generate 3D layouts and output articulated furniture as code (such as Articraft) has emerged. Modern frontier LLMs (such as GPT-6 and Claude Fable) also display impressive spatial reasoning and coding proficiency. Yet running these models out-of-the-box lacks an orchestration framework that can faithfully ground their reasoning in real-world RGB-D observations and reliably output sound physics-simulation scenes.

LiteReality-Agent resolves this gap. Its core concept treats room reconstruction as a programming challenge: authoring a script called Room.py. The system operates in two main stages—Scene Initialisation and Agentic Authoring. In the authoring stage, a tool-augmented coding agent runs an observe-edit-verify loop. Because the room is expressed purely as code, users can also easily modify the scene afterward using natural language, such as asking it to "add a laptop on the desk."

sections.heading: From 3D reconstruction to scene generation and agentic inverse graphics
sections.summary: This work builds upon real-to-sim indoor scene reconstruction, 3D object and articulation generation from images, and LLM-driven scene synthesis and inverse graphics. LiteReality-Agent unites these threads into the first full-fledged system grounded by RGB-D observations and closed-loop verification.
sections.details:
Related work broadly spans four areas:

### Indoor Reconstruction and Real-to-Sim
Beyond traditional CAD retrieval-and-placement and neural rendering (NeRF/3DGS), interactive scene reconstruction from video (such as DRAWER) and digital twin generation for robot learning (such as Phone2Proc, RialTo, and PolaRiS) have gained traction. However, they often stop at coarse meshes or struggle with articulation and accurate physics properties.

### Single-Object 3D Generation and Articulation
Techniques generating 3D meshes from single images (like TRELLIS.2) and methods that model parts and joints (hinges and sliders) via code (like Real2Code and Articraft) have matured significantly. This paper incorporates these strategies into its per-object asset reconstruction.

### Language-Guided 3D Authoring and Agentic Inverse Graphics
Approaches that instruct LLMs to write Blender scripts for scene assembly (such as SceneCraft and SceneSmith), alongside inverse graphics methods that inspect images to refine code (SceneScript, Thinking in Blender), have advanced rapidly.

LiteReality-Agent synthesizes these individual advances into a practical, end-to-end orchestration system. Grounded in consumer-grade RGB-D scans, it couples multi-view visual alignment with strict physical support and collision verification.

sections.heading: Observe, edit, and verify: how the system architecture works
sections.summary: LiteReality-Agent first establishes the room boundaries and initial furniture layout during Scene Initialisation, then refines the details through Agentic Authoring. Combining evidence gathering, rendering inspection, and geometric support quality gates, it produces a physically sound environment in Room.py.
sections.details:
### 3.1 & 3.2 Scene Initialisation
The pipeline begins with RGB-D scans and 3D bounding box detections from the LiteReality Scan companion app. First, the Layout Agent cleans up the noisy raw scan detections. It identifies boxes that penetrate walls, hover in mid-air, or unnaturally overlap, applying geometric checks and deterministic optimization or visual reasoning to refine placements. Crucially, its scene graph representation distinguishes legitimate overlaps—such as a chair tucked under a desk—from problematic collisions.

Next comes per-object reconstruction. Articulated or boxy geometric furniture is routed to procedural code generation (following Articraft), whereas complex static assets are reconstructed using an image-to-3D model (TRELLIS.2). Procedural assets are automatically assigned physical properties such as mass, inertia tensors, friction coefficients, and convex collision meshes. These components are then compiled into the initial Room.py.

### 3.3 Agentic Authoring
This is the core strength of the approach. The agent iteratively refines Room.py using several dedicated tools:
- **3-tier image selection and rendering inspection**: Compares real scan photos with current Blender renders side-by-side from identical camera poses across three scopes: whole-room, single-wall, or individual object.
- **Wall stitching and metric grid**: Stitches and undistorts wall views into a fronto-parallel composite with metric grid overlays. This lets the agent read exact physical coordinates, such as "the whiteboard is 1.2 m above the floor and 0.8 m from the wall edge," and translate them directly into code.
- **Modular schedule**: Authoring systematically moves through wall materials, fixtures and lights, small props, and procedural asset fine-tuning.

### 3.3.2 Budget Control and Quality Gates
To prevent the LLM from getting trapped in infinite loops, tool calls are bounded by a budget, and the final 10% of turns are dedicated strictly to saving and clean-up. Additionally, automated collision gates detect mesh intersections and support gates verify that object bases sit flush against floors or tables, forcibly correcting floating or penetrating furniture.

### 3.4 Simulation Export
The finalized scene is exported to MuJoCo. Static walls and fixtures are welded, articulated furniture pieces receive hinge or slide joints, and movable objects receive free joints, making the environment instantly ready for physics simulation.

sections.heading: How does it stack up against frontier LLMs and existing pipelines?
sections.summary: Benchmarked across 10 indoor scenes spanning 620 camera views (including offices, kitchens, and meeting rooms), LiteReality-Agent outperformed frontier model baselines (GPT-6, Claude Fable 5.1) and prior systems across visual fidelity, geometric precision, and human subjective ratings.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Baselines
Evaluations were conducted on 10 real-world scenes across 620 views. LiteReality-Agent was evaluated against the prior LiteReality method, GPT-6 Astra running in Codex, and Fable 5.1 running in Claude Code. General-purpose agent baselines were tested under two settings: "RGB-only" (photos only) and "+Scan" (provided with point clouds, depth, and RoomPlan bounding boxes, identical to our system).

### Visual Fidelity
Rendered images were evaluated against real photographs taken from the same camera poses. LiteReality-Agent achieved the highest scores across PSNR, SSIM, RMSE, and LPIPS. Compared to its strongest competitor, GPT-6 (+Scan), it improved PSNR by 1.162 dB and reduced perceptual error (LPIPS) by 13.7%. Against the prior LiteReality system, PSNR improved by a substantial 2.248 dB.

### Geometric Consistency and Physical Validity
Crucial for simulation, geometric and physical metrics showed stark contrasts:
- **Depth MAE (Mean Absolute Error)**: LiteReality-Agent achieved 10.50 cm, a 21.2% reduction compared to GPT-6 (+Scan) at 13.33 cm, and far outperforming LiteReality at 15.03 cm.
- **Bottom near-contact rate**: Across all 86 furniture items, 100% had their bases within 1 cm of their supporting surfaces (compared to 63.0% for GPT-6 +Scan).
- **Furniture mesh intersections**: The system achieved 0 intersecting surface pairs among detected furniture (versus 43 for LiteReality, 24 for GPT-6 +Scan, and 54 for Fable 5.1 +Scan). While giving scan data to generalist LLM agents improved their visual PSNR, it actually caused more furniture penetrations. This highlights the indispensable role of our domain-specific quality gates.

### Subjective Evaluation and Simulation Tasks
In a user study with 13 participants (5-point scale), LiteReality-Agent scored 4.60 in layout accuracy, 4.58 in object similarity, and 4.54 in overall similarity, easily beating baselines (which hovered between 2.9 and 3.1 for GPT-6 +Scan). Furthermore, in MuJoCo, a Franka robotic arm successfully executed pick-and-place manipulation tasks on reconstructed kitchen items, and drop tests confirmed that furniture settled naturally without explosive physics glitches.

captions.F4: Reconstruction results for a kitchen (top row) and meeting room (bottom row). Real RGB scans, our reconstructions, and overhead floor plans demonstrate that even tabletop wires and small props are structurally reproduced.
captions.F6: Scene re-editing and simulation applications. Lighting and furniture can be flexibly altered via natural language prompts or code edits, and exported into MuJoCo for Franka arm pick-and-place manipulation.

sections.heading: Takeaway: a major step toward a standard real-to-sim foundation
sections.summary: By framing 3D indoor reconstruction as a programming problem, LiteReality-Agent delivers visually accurate, geometrically sound digital twins ready for physics simulation. Serving as a robust orchestration harness that directly harnesses advancing coding agents, it represents an important asset for embodied AI.
sections.details: Rather than relying on a single black-box model, the true significance of this work lies in combining an executable script (Room.py), dedicated measurement and comparison tools, and rigorous quality gates that reject penetration and floating artifacts.\n\nAs the core abilities of LLMs and coding agents continue to advance, plugging them into this orchestration framework will naturally boost reconstructed scene quality. Because both the source code and data capture app are released open source, the system offers a practical, accessible real-to-sim foundation for the robotics research community.

sections.heading: Appendix: layout repair rules and object reconstruction details
sections.summary: The appendix details the layout repair constraints applied during initialization and the routing between procedural and generative 3D asset reconstruction. Structured scene graphs and constrained search completely eliminated initial bounding box anomalies.
sections.details:
### Concrete Constraints for Layout Repair
Because raw bounding box detections contain substantial noise, the Layout Agent uses a scene graph to perform constrained spatial adjustments:
- **Allowed translation and scaling**: Translations are bounded to 0.6 m horizontally and 0.08 m vertically. Resizing is restricted to within 15% per axis for primary furniture (tables, chairs, beds) and 35% for smaller props.
- **Coupled functional groups**: In office layouts, a table and its surrounding chairs are translated together by the same horizontal offset (e.g., 14.5 cm), resolving wall collisions while preserving relative seating relationships.
- **Repair track record**: Across 107 input bounding boxes, 29 were translated and 4 were resized, driving the number of layout checker errors from 30 down to 0.

### Two Object Reconstruction Pathways
For furniture reconstruction, generative image models first produce clean reference images free of reflections and sensor noise. Articulated assets like sinks and cabinets are then dispatched to procedural Python code generation, whereas complex static objects like sofas are routed to TRELLIS.2 mesh generation. If generated meshes exhibit flaws, an automated regeneration loop is triggered.

captions.F10: The two object reconstruction pathways. The sink cabinet on the left contains moving parts (doors) and is procedurally generated as Python code, while the red sofa on the right is reconstructed via image-to-3D mesh generation (TRELLIS.2).

takeaways: Treating 3D scene reconstruction as an ongoing refactoring task on a single executable Python script is a highly effective paradigm that plays directly to the strengths of LLM coding agents.

Visual fidelity (such as PSNR) and physical validity (penetration and grounding) often conflict; incorporating strict verification quality gates is essential to make reconstructed scenes viable for simulation.
Dedicated grounding tools, such as metric grid overlays on undistorted wall composites, are critical for enabling agents to accurately perceive and apply real-world dimensions.
limitations: Physical properties like mass and friction coefficients are estimated from category and material priors (LLM knowledge) rather than calibrated against dynamic real-world measurements.
While layout repair enforces geometric validity, severe errors in the initial scan bounding box detector (RoomPlan) can still result in discrepancies with the actual room layout.
Evaluation is currently limited to 10 rooms (620 views); scaling the system to multi-room residences or large, multi-story buildings remains an open area for future validation.
